title: When the Constitution Says Nothing Yet
hook: About 96,000 American children were born through IVF in 2023. The Supreme Court has barely addressed the technology — leaving state courts to invent the rules one dispute at a time.
key_points: IVF accounted for roughly 96,000 US births in 2023, about 2.3% of all births.
Cohen counts only three Supreme Court decisions touching IVF, none of which developed constitutional doctrine.
Meanwhile state courts decide surrogacy, frozen-embryo and provider-discrimination disputes continually.
Alabama's Supreme Court held in 2024 that improperly destroyed embryos counted as children under wrongful-death law, prompting fast legislative intervention.
A federal district court found Utah's surrogacy restrictions unconstitutional in J.R. v. Utah (2002) — a rare federal ruling in the area.
Cohen sketches three possible frameworks: traditionalist, equality-based, and liberationist.
content_html: Constitutional law is usually described as a set of answers. Just as often it is a set of silences — areas where the Supreme Court has simply never spoken, leaving no federal floor beneath which states cannot go. Writing at SCOTUSblog, Harvard's I. Glenn Cohen, who directs the Petrie-Flom Center for Health Law Policy, Biotechnology and Bioethics, argues that reproductive technology is one of the largest such silences.
extra_html:
The scale of the gap is what makes it striking. Roughly 96,000 children were born in the United States through IVF in 2023, about 2.3% of all births, and yet Cohen counts only three Supreme Court decisions that touch the technology at all — Webster v. Reproductive Health Services (1989), which noted IVF without addressing it; Astrue v. Capato (2012), which allowed a state to exclude posthumously conceived children from Social Security benefits; and the Dobbs dissent, which flagged future questions rather than answering any. State courts, by contrast, decide these disputes constantly: who owns a frozen embryo after a divorce, whether surrogacy contracts are enforceable, when a provider may refuse treatment.

The consequences of a vacuum are visible in Alabama, where the state supreme court held in 2024 that improperly destroyed embryos counted as children under the wrongful-death statute — a ruling whose implications for clinics produced immediate political backlash and legislative correction. Occasionally a federal court steps in, as in J.R. v. Utah (2002), where a district court found the state's surrogacy restrictions unconstitutional. Cohen's own view is that the silence is unhealthy for democracy, and he lays out three frameworks a court could eventually adopt: traditionalist, protecting only practices with deep historical roots; equality-based, protecting those with medical infertility; and liberationist, extending reproductive capability broadly, including to same-sex couples. Which one wins matters enormously — but the prior lesson is structural. Where the federal constitution is quiet, the operative law is whatever fifty state judiciaries happen to say.

related.title: Abortion After Dobbs
related.hook: In 2022 the Supreme Court did something rare: it withdrew a constitutional right it had recognized for half a century — and handed the question back to the states.

related.title: State Constitutions Can Guarantee More Than the Federal One Does
related.hook: The U.S. Constitution sets a floor of rights, not a ceiling. New York's constitution goes further — it makes aiding the needy a state duty, not just a policy choice.

related.title: Civil Liberties Basics
related.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

flashcards.prompt: What does Cohen mean by a federal 'constitutional vacuum'?
flashcards.back_html: The Supreme Court has never developed doctrine on reproductive technologies, so there is no federal floor of protection — and state courts and legislatures fill the space unevenly.

flashcards.prompt: What happened after the Alabama Supreme Court's 2024 embryo ruling?

choices.text: Political backlash followed and the legislature intervened
The US Supreme Court promptly reversed it
Every other state adopted the same rule

flashcards.explanation_html: The court held improperly destroyed embryos were children under wrongful-death law; the practical consequences for IVF clinics prompted swift legislative action.

flashcards.prompt: Which of Cohen's three candidate frameworks would protect only long-established practices?
flashcards.explanation_html: Traditionalist reasoning protects what is historically rooted; equality-based reasoning keys on medical infertility, while the liberationist view extends protection much more broadly.
